facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13 states; this is the date Georgia ratified the U.S. Constitution, the fourth state to do so.
facts.nickname: The Peach State (also the Empire State of the South)
facts.name_origin: Named for King George II of Great Britain, who issued the colony's charter in 1732.

government.chambers: Georgia State Senate (56 senators) and Georgia House of Representatives (180 representatives); members of both serve 2-year terms.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; may serve two terms in a row, then must wait four years before running again). The governor leads the executive branch; voters also elect a lieutenant governor separately.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Georgia (9 justices since a 2016 law added two seats; the constitution allows up to nine. The justices choose a chief justice, and justices are elected in nonpartisan elections for 6-year terms). The Court of Appeals also has statewide authority.
government.local: 159 counties, the second most of any state after Texas (Georgia had 161 until 1931, when Milton and Campbell counties joined Fulton).
government.constitution: Georgia's current constitution, its tenth, was ratified by voters on November 2, 1982, and took effect July 1, 1983. Before statehood, Georgia was run under a royal charter from 1732.
government.kid_line: "All government, of right, originates with the people, is founded upon their will only, and is instituted solely for the good of the whole." (Georgia Constitution, Article I, Section II, Paragraph I)

long_ago.about: From about 800 to 1500, towns such as Coosa and Ocute built flat-topped earthen mounds and grew large fields of corn. Etowah, near Cartersville, was lived in from about 1000 to 1550.
Ocmulgee, near Macon, is the ancestral homeland of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation. The Creek Confederacy joined many towns and peoples, including Hitchiti, Yuchi (Uchean) and Muscogee towns.

The Cherokee Nation's homeland included north Georgia. In the early 1800s the Cherokee ran their own government with a written constitution, a council and a supreme court, with New Echota in northwest Georgia as their capital from 1825.

long_ago.nation: The Guale and Yamacraw of the coast
long_ago.about: Small Muskogean-speaking nations lived along the coast. The Yamacraw, led by Tomochichi, lived on the bluff where Savannah is today.

today.about: Recognized by the Georgia legislature in 2007; not federally recognized.

first_peoples.today_note: The Muscogee (Creek) and Cherokee were forced out of Georgia in the 1830s, and their nations are based outside Georgia today: the federally recognized Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and the federally recognized Poarch Band of Creek Indians, in Alabama; the Cherokee Nation and United Keetoowah Band in Oklahoma; and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians in North Carolina. Georgia's legislature recognized three groups in 2007 that are not federally recognized, and the state's Council on American Indian Concerns, set up in 2001, works with Native communities.
sites: Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park, Macon (more than 12,000 years of human life; Muscogee homeland)
Etowah Indian Mounds Historic Site, near Cartersville (Mississippian town, 1000–1550)
New Echota, Gordon County, now a state historic site (Cherokee Nation capital and start of the Trail of Tears)

history.event: People are living at Ocmulgee, near present-day Macon, a place with more than 12,000 years of human life.
Mississippian towns such as Coosa, Ocute and Etowah build platform mounds and farm corn in villages.
Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto leads an army through the Southeast, meeting powerful nations such as Coosa and Ocute.
On February 12, the first English colonists arrive at what becomes Savannah. Tomochichi of the Yamacraw gives land on Yamacraw Bluff, and the colony is named for King George II.
Georgia's trustees ban slavery, the only British colony to do so, but the ban is overturned in 1749. By 1775 about 18,000 people are enslaved, a majority of the colony's people.
On January 2, Georgia ratifies the U.S. Constitution and becomes the fourth state.
After the Creek War, the Treaty of Fort Jackson forces the Creek to give up more than 21 million acres in what is now southern Georgia and central Alabama.
The Cherokee Nation makes New Echota its capital and starts the Cherokee Phoenix, printed in English and in Sequoyah's Cherokee writing system.
Gold is found in the north Georgia mountains, starting the Georgia Gold Rush. More white settlers arrive and pressure the U.S. government to force the Cherokee out.

The U.S. Supreme Court rules in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that Georgia cannot take over Cherokee lands, but Georgia and President Andrew Jackson ignore it. The Creek are forced west in 1836, and in 1838 soldiers round up the Cherokee and force them west on the Trail of Tears, where thousands die.
On January 19, Georgia secedes and joins the Confederacy. About 5,000 Georgians, Black and white, join the Union Army.
Union General William T. Sherman captures Atlanta and marches his army to Savannah, destroying railroads and farms along the way.

In January, Sherman's Special Field Orders No. 15 sets aside abandoned plantation land on the Sea Islands to be given to freed families in small plots, but President Andrew Johnson takes the land back later that year.
Atlanta becomes the capital. White lawmakers refuse to seat Henry McNeal Turner and 26 other newly elected Black legislators; they are reinstated in January 1870 under federal military rule.

trailblazers.name: Tomochichi
trailblazers.text: Head chief of a Yamacraw town where Savannah stands today, he gave land on Yamacraw Bluff for the new town and became the main peacemaker between Native people and the English settlers. In 1734 he traveled to England and met King George II, giving him eagle feathers as a sign of peace.

trailblazers.name: Mary Musgrove (Coosaponakeesa)
trailblazers.group: Muscogee and English woman, interpreter and trader
trailblazers.text: Born at the Creek town of Coweta to a Muscogee mother and an English father, she ran trading posts and served as interpreter, go-between and adviser to James Oglethorpe for about ten years, helping arrange treaties between the Creek and the colony.

trailblazers.name: John Ross (Guwisguwi)
trailblazers.text: He was Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation from 1828 to 1866, longer than anyone else. He led the nation through its fight against removal, the Trail of Tears and the Civil War.

trailblazers.name: Ellen and William Craft
trailblazers.group: Black American freedom seekers and abolitionists
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Macon, they escaped in December 1848 by train and steamboat. Ellen disguised herself as a white planter, a man, and William pretended to be her servant; they reached Philadelphia on Christmas Day and later spoke out against slavery.

trailblazers.name: Susie King Taylor
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, nurse and teacher
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Liberty County, she became the first African American nurse in the Civil War, caring for soldiers of the 1st South Carolina Volunteers (33rd U.S. Colored Troops). After the war she opened a school for Black children and adults in Savannah, and in 1902 she published a book about her life.

trailblazers.name: Henry McNeal Turner
trailblazers.text: He was the first African American chaplain in the U.S. Colored Troops. In 1868 Macon voters elected him to the Georgia legislature, but white lawmakers refused to seat him and 26 other Black members until the federal government stepped in. He later became a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

trailblazers.name: Juliette Gordon Low
trailblazers.group: Woman leader, founder of the Girl Scouts
trailblazers.text: Born in Savannah, she started the first Girl Guide troop in the United States there in 1912; it became the Girl Scouts. She was deaf in one ear after an infection and had partial hearing loss from childhood.

landforms: Blue Ridge Mountains (Brasstown Bald, 4,783 feet, is the highest point)
Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians and the Cumberland Plateau in the northwest
Barrier islands such as Cumberland, Sapelo and the Golden Isles
waters: Okefenokee Swamp (headwaters of the Suwannee and St. Marys rivers)
geography.regions: Georgia has five natural regions: the Cumberland Plateau and the Ridge-and-Valley in the northwest corner, the Blue Ridge Mountains in the north, the Piedmont plateau in the middle, and the wide Atlantic Coastal Plain in the south and along the coast.

ecosystems.name: Okefenokee Swamp
ecosystems.about: A shallow, 438,000-acre, peat-filled wetland and the largest blackwater swamp in North America. It is famous for its frogs and other amphibians and is home to threatened and endangered animals like the red-cockaded woodpecker, indigo snake and wood stork; in 2026 it became Georgia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

ecosystems.name: Salt marsh and barrier islands
ecosystems.about: On Sapelo Island, smooth cordgrass covers about 90 percent of the reserve's 4,000 acres of tidal salt marsh, where egrets, herons and fiddler crabs live. Cumberland Island is Georgia's largest and southernmost barrier island, shaped by wind and fire.

ecosystems.name: Forests from mountains to coast
ecosystems.about: Georgia has about 250 kinds of trees, including pines, oaks, cypress, sweetgum and live oaks. White-tailed deer live in nearly every county, and about 160 kinds of birds, including the brown thrasher, live in the state.

science.weather: Most of Georgia has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers. Georgia is one of the leading states for how often tornadoes happen, though most are weak. Hurricanes rarely hit the coast directly, but storms that cross Florida, like Hurricane Michael, can bring strong winds and heavy rain inland.
science.resources: Georgia raises more chickens for food than any other state and grows more pecans than anywhere in the world, plus peanuts, corn, soybeans and blueberries. Manufacturing and the film industry are also big parts of the economy.
science.highlight: Right whale nursery! Each fall some North Atlantic right whales swim more than 1,000 miles south to the shallow waters off Georgia and its neighbors to give birth. Calves are about 14 feet long at birth, and the right whale is Georgia's state marine mammal.

g3_ss.title: Georgia's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Atlanta, learn what the governor and General Assembly do, count Georgia's 159 counties, and read Article I, Section II, Paragraph I of the state constitution.

g3_ss.title: Georgia's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the mound builders of Ocmulgee and Etowah, the Muscogee (Creek) and the Cherokee, and learn where these nations live today.

g3_ss.title: Georgia Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Tomochichi, Ellen and William Craft, Susie King Taylor and Juliette Gordon Low, and ask what new path each one opened.

g45_ss.title: Georgia's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Use Ocmulgee and Etowah to study Mississippian towns, then compare Muscogee and Cherokee life, and read the Cherokee Phoenix as a primary source.

g45_ss.title: Colonial Georgia: Tomochichi, Oglethorpe and the Slavery Ban
g45_ss.plan: Trace the 1733 founding of Savannah with Tomochichi and Mary Musgrove, the trustees' ban on slavery and why it was overturned, and ratification in 1788.

g45_ss.title: Georgia 1788–1877: Removal, War and Reconstruction
g45_ss.plan: Study the Treaty of Fort Jackson, the gold rush, Worcester v. Georgia and the Trail of Tears, the Crafts' escape, the Civil War and Sherman's march, Field Orders No. 15, and Henry McNeal Turner and the Black legislators of 1868.

g3_sci.title: The Okefenokee Swamp
g3_sci.plan: Explore a blackwater swamp, meet its frogs, alligators and wading birds, and learn why it became a World Heritage Site.

g3_sci.title: Salt Marsh and Barrier Islands
g3_sci.plan: Visit Sapelo and Cumberland islands (virtually), meet fiddler crabs and cordgrass, and see how marshes and dunes protect the coast.

g3_sci.title: Storms in Georgia
g3_sci.plan: Learn how thunderstorms, tornadoes and hurricanes form, chart Georgia weather, and practice family safety plans.

g45_sci.title: Georgia's Five Regions from Mountains to Coast
g45_sci.plan: Compare rocks, soils, plants and animals in the Blue Ridge, Ridge-and-Valley, Cumberland Plateau, Piedmont and Coastal Plain.

g45_sci.title: Right Whales of the Georgia Coast
g45_sci.plan: Use migration and calf-count data to explain why right whales travel to Georgia's coast to give birth and what threatens them.

g45_sci.title: Wetlands at Work
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how the Okefenokee and coastal salt marshes store water, filter it and support food webs, using real refuge data.
